### Q1: It can be found that most dense retrieval models (including MoMA-DR w/o Target) performs worse than BM25 (a very simple baseline) and even MoMA-DR exceeds BM25 with a slight margin. What's the cause for this phenomenon? Is the source training corpus (MS MARCO passage) and/or being unrelated to the BEIR datasets?

A1: 
The phenomenon can be traced to the intrinsic difficulty of zero-shot dense retrieval.
In fact, early DR methods show strong performances first in supervised settings, but failed to outperform BM25 in zero-shot because of domain shifts. 
Even today, BM25 remains a competitive ZeroDR method, being the backbone of successful industrial search engine services such as elasticsearch (https://www.elastic.co/elasticsearch) and Azure Cognitive Search (https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/free/cognitive-search/
).
Only recently, research in dense retrieval elevate the zero-shot accuracy to outperform BM25, i.e. the several baselines in this paper.

The web search domain is one of the best source domain to train dense retrieval models. It is a general domain that has certain overlaps with specific domains, for example, there are many medical queries in commercial web search. It is also a scenario where a large amount of supervision labels are avaialble, such as user clicks.
Previous research [1] demonstrates this in the academic setting, MS MARCO, a general domain web search benchmark, is an effective source corpus, in comparison to other general web domain corpus like NQ.
We agree with the reviewers that the semantic gap between source (MARCO) and target (BEIR) is a key challenge in zero-shot dense retrieval. The same challenge also exists in real world retrieval systems. That is exactly the challenge this work as well as recent efforts in dense retrieval focus on.

### Q2: Besides, it can be found in Table 2 that the target dataset is the core for MoMA-DR compared to external corpus (i.e., the 5th column versus the 8th column, 0.431 versus 0.436), which weakens the claim that multiple external corpus used in MoMA is helpful for zeroDR. Is it possible to make some case study to show that the external corpus does contribute some knowledge that is uncovered in the target dataset?

A2: As shown in Table 2 in our paper, the trend of MoMA effectiveness with ''Target'',  ''w/o Target'', and ''Full'' settings is intuitive. The target domain information is the richest and should be the most valuable resource to improve target domain zero-shot accuracy. That said, using the mixture of memory in addition to target still yield better zero-shot performance.
At the same time, we also observe significant gains without Target ''w/o target'' over ''no Memory''. This is another benefit of MoMA. In certain real world scenarios, the target tasks' information is completely hidden from the deployed system, for example, due to privacy and security reasons. This is a common setting in transfer learning, namely ''domain generalization''. 
Table 4 in our paper show some case studies on the effectiveness of external corpora. 

[1] Xin et al. Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval with Momentum Adversarial Domain Invariant Representations. ACL Findings 2022.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors proposed a mixture-of-memory augmentation framework for a zero-shot dense retrieval (MoMA-DR). The key idea is to enrich the query representation with external resources such as wiki, knowledge graphs, etc. The framework consists of two components: a retrieval model and an augmentation model. The retrieval model follows the usual dense retriever settings, and the augmentation model is used to select some relevant/useful documents from external resources for query representation enrichment. To verify the effectiveness of this idea, they conducted experiments on the BEIR benchmark datasets and showed that it could provide some performance boost.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength:
- Making the query augmentation process trainable and automatic is interesting and novel in the current dense retrieval field.  The iterative joint optimization mechanism of the retrieval model and the augmentation model is natural. 
- Detailed study on the impact of different memories and the joint learning mechanism.
-The paper is easy to follow and well-orgnaized.

### Weaknesses:
- This idea is similar to query augmentation methods [a], but it seems that this related line of research is not well explained and reviewed in the paper. 
- Preparing the external resource is not a trivial thing (the impact varies on different datasets). Important questions about this, such as what resources to include and where to find them, are not answered. Given the difficulty of finding suitable external resources and the high cost of maintaining them, the applicability/effectiveness of this framework is limited.
- The reported performance is not that promising. Compared with a recent work contriever [b], this model performs much worse. Also, if we include hybrid models such as BM25+CE, the results of MoMA-DR are even less attractive. 


- [a] A Survey of Automatic Query Expansion in Information Retrieval, CSUR, 2012
- [b] Unsupervised Dense Information Retrieval with Contrastive Learning, JMLR, 2021
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity
I do have a few questions that may need clarification from the authors:
- What is the computational cost of the proposed framework in terms of training and inference, and how is it compared with other approaches? In my understanding, if the augmentation corpus is very large (e.g., much larger than the corpus of interest), the process of retrieving augmented documents can be very costly. And this process can not be taken offline as it is query specific.
- Could you give more details on the "BM25 warmed-up T5 retriever"?
- What is the impact of K and N? Why not tune them? Does tuning them bring additional benefits or worsen the model?
- What are the training datasets of these dense retriever baselines?

### Reproducibility
The source code is not available.

The performance improvement is not that encouraging. Some related work and stronger baselines are not included for discussion/comparison. The expensive augmentation process is done online, which can heavily limit its use in practical/industrial environments.

### Q1: This idea is similar to query augmentation methods [a], but it seems that this related line of research is not well explained and reviewed in the paper.

A1: 
From the IR perspective, the application of retrieval augmentation on query side is a form of query expansion.
The major difference between ours and previous augmentation methods is the augmentation in MoMA-DR is performed in the embedding space with external knowledge.
One related work in this field is ANCE-PRF [1], which appends top retrieval results directly to the end of original queries. 
Different from ANCE-PRF, we introduce knowledge in a fusion-in-decoder manner from multiple corpora, and we perform better than ANCE-PRF (which can be validated from the ``MSMARCO'' entry in our ablation study Table 2).

Another thread of related work in IR is those that introduce external knowledge to improve the query expansion [e.g., 2], MoMA-DR introduce external knowledge from multiple corpora and perform the operation in the modern dense retrieval setup.

Thanks for the review, we will add a related related work paragraph discussing the query augmentation/expansion method.

### Q2: Preparing the external resource is not a trivial thing (the impact varies on different datasets). Important questions about this, such as what resources to include and where to find them, are not answered. Given the difficulty of finding suitable external resources and the high cost of maintaining them, the applicability/effectiveness of this framework is limited.

A2: MoMA can actually be used as a tool for users to customize the system with their domain knowledge, while without requiring extensive AI/CS skills. For example, a user with medical background can pick the medical corpus that she considered important for her search scenario to improve the retrieval accuracy. This can be done without retraining the model with MoMA. 
In case they do not have domain knowledge, we provide the default strategies that include a set of corpora that cover a wide range of potential scenarios, as described in this paper.

For all memory component described in this paper, we provide sources and detailed statistics in Appendix A.1.
In total, our augmentation corpora consume less than 50GB CPU memories, which is a typical memory load for modern retrieval systems.

### Q3: The reported performance is not that promising. Compared with a recent work contriever [b], this model performs much worse. Also, if we include hybrid models such as BM25+CE, the results of MoMA-DR are even less attractive.

A3: We provide a detailed discussion between MoMA-DR and ColBERT in General Response Q1.
As illustrated in General Response Table 1, Contriever is contrastively trained on CCNet, a large corpus with 1.5 billions documents in 174 languages using 2K batches for 500k steps, while MoMA-DR's improvement mainly comes from the memory augmentation technique.
To demonstrate MoMA-DR can also integrate techniques from other models to achieve higher performances, we apply MoMA with a better pretrained T5 model, which is continuously pretrained on the MARCO corpus using standard T5 masked language modeling loss for 50k steps with batch size 128, a weaker version compared to the techniques used in the ``additional training corpora'' row in Table 1. 
General Response Table 2 shows that MoMA-DR (MARCO MLM) achieving the highest average scores, outperforming other methods on the BEIR benchmark. This confirms that MoMA-DR can flexibly pair with other techniques in Table 1 to obtain higher empirical results, when needed in real world systems.

BM25+CE perform reranking on top of the retrieval results. 
We do not include reranking methods as it is the future stage after retrieval in the IR pipeline.
Rerankers can be added on top of retrieval results and a lot of research papers show it helps. One can build a reranking layer upon our retrieval system as well if needed.
Comparison of L1 retrieval + L2 reranking system with a system with only L1 component is unfair.

### Q4: What is the computational cost of the proposed framework in terms of training and inference?

A4: We summarize the online serving and offline model training overhead and compare it with baselines in General Response Table 3 and 4.
Please refer to the General Response Q2 for detailed analysis.
In short, 1) our offline training is significantly cheaper 2) our online imposes a necessary cost of retrieval augmented model but is within an acceptable range because a) MoMA-DR online encoding is efficient b) the ANN operation is very fast and is sublinear w.r.t. corpus size.

### Q5: Could you give more details on the "BM25 warmed-up T5 retriever"?

A5: Recent research found MARCO passage training labels and BM25 negatives can help train dense retrieval model.
Following ANCE, GTR and coCondenser, our models are first trained using MARCO official released BM25 Negatives.
BM25 warmed-up is a standard practice adopted in dense retrieval. 
We will add more details in the paper.

### Q6: What is the impact of K and N? Why not tune them? Does tuning them bring additional benefits or worsen the model?

A6: $K$ controls the number of augmentation documents.
Higher $K$ means more knowledge from augmentation, which possibly increases performances with a higher computational cost.
$N$ controls how greedily we want our model to learn from the aggregated attention scores, higher $N$ includes more top ranked documents as pseudo training labels for the augmentation component.
Tuning the parameters likely will result in more gains.
Unfortunately, it is expensive as each time it re-trains on the source domain and then tests separately on 18 target datasets.
We initially set the two values and observe performance improvement, so we stick with the two values to make sure the gains are from the main contribution not engineering.

### Q7: What are the training datasets of these dense retriever baselines?

A7: We add more details in Table 1.

### Q8: The source code is not available.

A8: We add the source code in the Supplementary Material.

content.comment:
### Q1: Generalizable retrieval augmented language model were proposed by [1] and it does also covers zero-shot scenario (e.g. Table 6) and the idea is a bit similar. I encourage authors to discuss and compare thoroughly.

A1: Atlas [1] is a concurrent work to MoMA-DR.
The two works focus on different aspects of retrieval-augmentation:
Atlas studies few-shot learning with better retrieval augmentation;
MoMA-DR focuses on developing a  plug-in-and-play model to retrieve from multiple corpora.
We also include a strong version of Atlas (i.e., attention distillation (ADist)) as a baseline and analyze why it leads to sub-optimal results in Figure 2 and Table 3.
Our results show that simply applying Atlas under the mixture of memory setting cannot balance different sources of augmentation corpus very well and leads to less effective zero-shot generalization. Our technique that mines pseudo positive documents and pair it up with hard negatives is necessary for stable performance.

Apart from the joint training techniques, MoMA-DR differs from Atlas in the following aspects:
- **Motivation**: MoMA-DR studies how to learn from different grounding corpora; Atlas focuses on how to learn a better retrieve-augmented language model
- **Goal**: MoMA-DR studies zero-shot generalization ability and utilizes dense retrieval as a test bed; Atlas mainly focuses on the few-shot performances across different knowledge intensive tasks 
- **Setting**: MoMA-DR studies how to leverage retrieval augmentation signals from multiple corpora, where most corpora (except the source corpus) are without any direct supervision; Altas mainly focuses on single augmentation source.

Thanks for the suggestion from the reviewer, we will expand the related work section to discuss more details of Altas.

### Q2: Since the embedding function $f_a$, needs to be compatible with the new corpus, it is undeniable this method implicitly has some assumptions to the new corpora. For example, if $f_a$ performs only on the text inputs, a new corpora with product hierarchy codes will not work well.

A2: MoMA-DR is flexible to incorporate new modality, as many other modalities are being handled by adapted language model as well.
For example, Amazon product catalog can be modeled by flatten the structure [2]. 
Similarly, we could use CodeT5 [3] for code retrieval, MolT5 [4] for molecular retrieval, and Flamingo [5] to fit CV with language, etc.
We believe the same framework can be effective.
Meanwhile, studying the transferring between different modalities is also an interesting and promising future research direction. This work focuses on the language front.

### Q3: Since the proposed work assumes there is a given retrieval stack, comparing to the model with a similar number of parameters in DNN is not fair. The size of the database should be also considered for the fair comparison.

A3: We summarize the overhead of MoMA-DR and compare it with baselines in General Response Table 3 and 4.
Please refer to the General Response Q2 for detailed analysis.
In short, the ANN operation on the memory mixture is very fast and is sublinear w.r.t. corpus size.
Besides, our offline training is significantly cheaper than models with similar or less number of parameters.

### Q4: Since this paper heavily relies on retrieval-augmented language models, authors should also empirically compare to some popular retrieval-augmented models (RETRO/REALM/FiD).

A4: We compare MoMA-DR with a more advanced version of FiD in Section 5.3 Table 3 (the Row "ADist") as well as the vanilla FiD (the row ``w/o Distilling (Fixed)'')
As shown in the table, MoMA-DR outperforms both versions of FiD.
RETRO is a token-level retrieval augmented models designed mainly for the language modeling task which is different from document-level augmentations, as we discussed in the related work section.
Besides, RETRO hasn't release their checkpoints and corpora, and its scale makes is infeasible for most places to reproduce it.
Similarly, REALM mainly focuses on language modeling.
More importantly, REALM concatenates the augmentation documents with the main texts which is hard to leverage multiple documents due to sequence length limitations.

content.title: (Continued)
content.comment:
### Q5: I am not sure why ColBERT cannot be part of the comparison. It is actually much smaller than MoMA-DR and even without any database (but it largely outperforms on many tasks?).

A5: From Table 2, MoMA-DR outperforms ColBERT on the average of all BEIR tasks (MoMA-DR 0.445 VS ColBERT 0.431).
Although ColBERT is comparable with MoMA-DR in model size, it adds computational cost through other operations:
- Using multiple vectors for each token and Performing term-level similarity matching. 
In ColBERT, every query term embedding interacts with all document term embeddings via a MaxSim operator.
It further decomposes a single query and document vector into multiple word- or phrase- centered vectors.
The q-d matching is performed over multiple vectors, which is computationally expensive when the retrieval corpus reaches million level. It can easily enlarges the ANN index by ten or more times.
- Training on the larger TREC-CAR apart from MARCO.
Apart from training on MARCO, they additionally trained it on TREC-CAR, which includes 29M passages and 3M queries.
Compared to ColBERT, our training data is significantly small.
We only trained on MARCO with 0.5M queries and passages.

[1] Izacard et al. "Few-shot learning with retrieval augmented language models". arXiv preprint arXiv:2208.03299 (2022).

[2] Jeronymo et al. "A Boring-yet-effective Approach for the Product Ranking Task
of the Amazon KDD Cup 2022". In KDD Cup 2022 Workshop: ESCI
Challenge for Improving Product Search (2022).

[3] Wang et al. "CodeT5: Identifier-aware Unified Pre-trained Encoder-Decoder Models for Code Understanding and Generation". In EMNLP 2021.

[4] Edwards et al. "Translation between Molecules and Natural Language". In EMNLP 2022.

[5] Alayrac et al. "Flamingo: a Visual Language Model for Few-Shot Learning". In NeurIPS 2022.

## Updated Overall Performance
### Q1: MoMA-DR does not achieve strong enough performance gain over several baselines, e.g., Contriever, ColBERT, or GTR_large.

A1: These techniques focus on different stages of ZeroDR systems, and are not fair comparisons from the research perspective.
To illustrate, we show a breakdown of techniques used by different systems in Table 1.
As illustrated, other approaches uses one or more parallel techniques while MoMA-DR's improvement mainly comes from the memory augmentation technique.
Among the parallel techniques, some leads to a significant computational overhead.
For example, Contriever is contrastively trained on CCNet, a huge corpus with 1.5 billions documents in 174 languages using 2K batches for 500k steps.
Besides, some methods (e.g., GTR) perform dense retrieval training directly on the target corpus NQ, which makes it a different setup than ours.
Instead of integrating those techniques to chase the empirical results, 
we chose to keep things simple and make the research findings more clear than a heavily engineered system.

Table 1: Comparison of data and techniques used by different models.
 | Techniques  | coCondenser | GenQ  | ColBERT | Contriever |  GTR |  MoMA-DR |
 |:---   |    :----:   |   :----:  |    :----:    |    :----:   |   :----:  |   ---: |
 |Continuous Pretrain Corpora  | MARCO | n  | n | Wikipedia, CCNet |  CQA |  n |
 |Source Finetuning Corpora  | MARCO | MARCO  | MARCO | MARCO |  MARCO,NQ  |  n |
 |Contrastive Pretraining  | y | n  | n | y |  n |  n |
 |Data Augmentation  | y | y  | n | y |  y |  n |
 |Multiple Vectors Per Document  | n | n  | y | n |  n |  n |
 |Scale Up Parameters  | n | n  | n | n |  y |  n |
 |Memory Augmentation | n | n  | n | n |  n |  y |

That said, as a plug-in-and-play method, MoMA can also be combined with other techniques.
To demonstrate it can integrate techniques from other models to achieve higher performances, we apply MoMA with a better pretrained T5 model, which is continuously pretrained on the MARCO corpus using standard T5 masked language modeling loss for 50k steps with batch size 128, a weaker version compared to the techniques used in the ``additional training corpora'' row. 
We then performed the same MoMA training on top of the continuously pretrained T5 checkpoint and denoted it as MoMA-DR (MARCO MLM).
Since MARCO contains only 0.5M documents, it adds fewer computational overhead compared to other methods listed in the table, e.g., Contriever.

## Efficiency Analysis
### Q2: I'm curious to understand the system performance overhead (flops, training step time, serving latency etc) introduced by this mixture of memory method. How do the MoMA compare to other baseline models in terms of efficiency?

We evaluate the efficiency of MoMA-DR in two stages: offline model training and online inference.
1) In offline training, MoMA-DR **is significantly cheaper than other methods** as we do not require pretraining on external corpus.
Table 3 compares the training cost of MoMA-DR with other baselines.
The original MoMA-DR does not require pretraining on large external corpora, which saves hundreds of hours training time.
The improved MoMA-DR (MARCO MLM) additionally pretrain on MARCO for 50k steps, which is far fewer than the other compared methods. 
In MoMA-DR training, the bulk of computing is to update the embeddings of the training corpus using new checkpoints. 
This can be integrated with the negative construction in ANCE.

Table 3: Computational analysis in the  pretraining stage of different models.

| Model        | Pretraining Corpus | Batch Size | Training Steps |
|---------------------|-----------------------------|---------------------|-------------------------|
| MoMA-DR             | 0                           | 0                   | 0                       |
| MoMA-DR (MARCO MLM) | MARCO                       | 128                 | 50k                     |
| GTR                 | NQ, CQA                     | 2048                | 800k                    |
| Contriever          | CCNet                       | 2048                | 500k                    |
|                     | Wikipedia                   | 2048                | 200k                    |


2) In online inference, similar with other retrieval enhanced language models (e.g., RETRO, REALM, and FiD), MoMA-DR **imposes a necessary cost of retrieval augmented model** upon the baseline T5-ANCE. 
We further provide detailed efficiency analysis on MoMA-DR in Table 4.
The online latency is measured on one query and 100 retrieved documents. 
Due to the query augmentation, query encoding is more costly and takes about 55ms per query. 
Even with the augmentation cost, the full dense retrieval total online inference cost is 64ms, only slightly above the BM25 retrieval latency.
**The ANN retrieval is very efficient**, only takes 9ms. In addition, the complexity of ANN retrieval is sub-linear to the corpus size, in most ANN framework such as FAISS. Thus the extra round of ANN retrieval operation in MoMA-DR is not the bottleneck even when the size of memory mixture scales up.

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
The paper introduces a new method to improve zero-shot retrieval ability of dense retrievers. The main contribution is to enrich the query representation by using additional external resources, such as Wikipedia or knowledge bases, from which “augmentation documents” are retrieved and added to the query.

Most of the scores of the reviews for this paper are slightly below the acceptance threshold. Some of the concerns raised by the reviewers are the following. The proposed method is not well situated compared to relevant existing works, and this makes it hard for the reviewers to know what are the main contributions of the paper. Moreover, the paper feels a bit incremental, and the experimental results are not very strong compared to existing baselines. Finally, several reviewers raised concerns about claims made in the paper that should be clarified. For these reasons, I recommend to reject the paper, so that these concerns can be thoroughly addressed by the authors.
